question: Why did raising the P share from 0.4 to 0.6 at a P/Fe/Na ratio with Fe = 5 lengthen the defluidization time?
expect: premise false: 0.6/5/1 gave a SHORTER defluidization time than 0.4/5/1; high P weakened Fe's inhibitory effect (abstract; sec. 3.2)
rendered:
The document "Co-Incineration of Real Municipal Sewage Sludge in a Fluidized Bed: Effects of the Coexistence of P, Fe, and Na on Agglomeration and Heavy Metal Emissions" holds the answer to this question.

The key to answering this question is to understand the relationship between the P share, the P/Fe/Na ratio, and the defluidization time. 

When the P share was raised from 0.4 to 0.6 at a P/Fe/Na ratio with Fe = 5, it led to a decrease in the defluidization time. This is because the excess P overflows the iron-binding capacity, reacts with K and then with Na to form highly viscous low-melting-point metaphosphates, which form liquid bridges that override the structural stabilization of Fe.

Therefore, raising the P share from 0.4 to 0.6 at a P/Fe/Na ratio with Fe = 5 shortened the defluidization time, not lengthened it.
